description:
I saw a coyote at approximately 1 PM. I was at the Memory Care center, 14400 E Belleview Ave, 
Aurora, CO 80015. I went out to scare the coyote away from traffic, probably not smart. Upon returning the Maintenance man indicated the coyote lived there and was seen frequently. Luckily for me the coyote was not aggressive. The location is east of Good Will.

I believe I startled a couple of (perhaps young) resting coyotes as I walked our property this morning. I heard coyotes yipping last night (not uncommon here). We don't see them too often, but do hear them at night from time to time. As I walked up our hill, I saw two animals maybe 15-20 meters uphill from me. I only saw their blondish hind quarters as they disappeared  into the brush, but coyote is all that fits what I saw. 

I heard the Colo. Public Radio story on the Denver Coyote Project yesterday. What was intriguing to me and led me to report this sighting was that the animals immediately ran away from me. This location is within some 100-200 meters of the area where a neighbor killed two coyotes that he said broke off from pursuing a deer to pursue him while he was hunting in this area this past fall (probably November). So, what may be interesting here is two (now dead) coyotes reported to behave in an unusually aggressive manner in essentially the same area where two other coyotes quickly took off running away from me as I approached the area where they may have been resting this morning.

If you'd like additional information or are interested in studying coyotes in this area, let me know. I work with USFWS in Lakewood (deputy director of the Upper Colorado River Endangered Fish Recovery Program) and can be contacted at angela_kantola@fws.gov or granitesquirrel@gmail.com, 303-588-4074 (cell), 303-697-5059, or 303-236-9882 (office). 

My neighbors in this area know each other fairly well. Many are hunters. In addition to myself, I expect some neighbors could be convinced to cooperate with CPW/CSU on a coyote study if this area is of interest to you.

description:
I photographed this Coyote on the remote desert grasslands of Otero Mesa, NM.  They often don't mind people, so I largely ignored it.  While I had my lifer Baird's Sparrow _in view_ between the grasses, I noticed this Coyote was fairly close, so I took a few photos.  Then I thought to myself, "You've wanted to see a Baird's Sparrow for years, you drove over 7 hours to come out here to find one, you slept in the backseat of your car, you've been searching grasslands for over 5 hours already today, and now you're taking your eyes off of this amazing bird to photograph a mammal??"  My attention returned to my quarry, but the Coyote was walking my direction.  Once it got about 25 feet away, I yelled, "Boo!" and it jumped, but kept approaching.  I kept eye-contact with the Coyote, and when it was about 15 feet away, I repeated, "Boo!," and then it started running toward me.  Luckily, I found a Choya log on the ground next to me, and wielded it over my head.  At that last moment, that caused the Coyote to stop and then flee.

I wonder if he thought I had food, or if he thought I was challenging him, and that he could take me.  Very strange experience.  Needless to say, he flushed my sparrow.

NUMBER: 20191225
SPECIES: Coyote, Canis latrans Say, 1823[1]
DATE, TIME: 25 December 2019, 1 PM
CONDITION: Skinny with missing fur and crusty, scaly skin (Sarcoptic Mange).[2] Obviously sick and starving (Gier et al., 1978).
SIZE: adult
LOCALITY: Sol y Lomas, Santa Fe, New Mexico 87505 USA
LATITUDE, LONGITUDE: 35º38’33.00” N, 105º55’58.44” W (35.6425, -105.9329)
HABITAT: dry woods
ALTITUDE: 334.3 m (7500 ft, 1.42 mi)
BEHAVIOR: A couple drove up for our Christmas party, but mysteriously did not get out of their car.  Finally, their son went out to check on them and ‘rescued’ them from a coyote beside their car.  Once they came in and told us, EHW eased outside with a camera.  He saw the animal but did not obtain decent photos.
The animal must have been attracted by the smell of the foods the couple was bringing to the party.  Murray et al. (2015) and ACP (2017) noted Coyotes with serious mange, in desperation, seek out anthropogenic (human sourced) food.  Dry dog food had been put out in the yard for American Crows, Corvus brachyrhynchos Brehm, 1822.  The Coyote had tracked all over the area, but apparently, and oddly, did not eat the dog food.
	Coyotes are nocturnal and active at dawn and dusk.  However, ones with severe mange are active during the day (Otto, 2017) as was the present specimen.
OTHER SPECIES: EHW saw a Desert Cottontail, Sylvilagus audubonii (Baird, 1858), in the area.  Thus, appropriate prey was available.  The Canine Burrowing Mite,[4] Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis causes mange.
PHOTOGRAPHS: Earl Myers took a good photo of the Coyote (Fig. A).
COMMENTS: Kessler (2017) suggested that Coyotes consume small mammals impaired by warfarin[3] (rat poison).  This usually does not kill Coyotes (except in many, multiple doses), but may cause them to be more susceptible to other diseases such as mange.  This may help to explain the increases in mange.  These cases are in an upscale community where the use of warfarin-containing products is probably common.
IMPORTANCE: Mite infections (and thus mange) were once rare in Coyotes (Gier et al., 1978), but now have become more common, destructive, and worthy of documentation.  There was also mange in Coyotes in this same locality late last December.
